es.summary: Proteínas de membrana que se unen a opioides y modulan la transmisión del dolor y otras funciones fisiológicas.
key_points: Se localizan principalmente en el SNC y el tracto gastrointestinal.
Tres subtipos clínicos: μ (mu), κ (kappa) y δ (delta).
La activación produce analgesia, sedación y depresión respiratoria.
Uso crónico genera tolerancia, dependencia y posible síndrome de abstinencia.
Los antagonistas bloquean los receptores y revierten la sobredosis.

mechanism: Los opioides se unen al sitio activo del receptor y inhiben la liberación de neurotransmisores excitatorios.
La activación de μ reduce la transmisión nociceptiva en la médula espinal.
κ y δ modulan la percepción del dolor y la respuesta emocional.
La señalización disminuye la actividad de la adenilato ciclasa y abre canales de K⁺, hiperpolarizando la neurona.
nursing_care: Evaluar frecuencia respiratoria y nivel de conciencia antes y después de administrar opioides.
Monitorear SpO₂ y presión arterial cada 15‑30 min durante la fase aguda.
Retener la dosis y notificar al médico si la frecuencia respiratoria <12 rpm o SpO₂ <92%.
Mantener equipo de reanimación y naloxona a mano.
Documentar signos de depresión respiratoria, somnolencia excesiva o náuseas.
patient_teaching: Informar que la analgesia puede venir acompañada de somnolencia y estreñimiento.
Enseñar a no combinar opioides con alcohol, benzodiacepinas u otros depresores del SNC.
Explicar la importancia de reportar dificultad para respirar o cambios en el nivel de conciencia.
Indicar que no deben compartir su medicación y que deben almacenar los opioides en un lugar seguro.
antidote_overdose: Naloxona 0.4‑2 mg IV/IM/SC; repetir cada 2‑3 min hasta revertir depresión respiratoria.
Administrar soporte ventilatorio si la respiración no se restablece rápidamente.

care_plans.diagnosis: Riesgo de disminución de la perfusión tisular cardíaca
outcomes: Patrón respiratorio: frecuencia respiratoria ≥12 rpm en 24 h

interventions.action: Monitorizar frecuencia respiratoria cada 2 min durante la primera hora después de la dosis.
interventions.rationale: Detectar depresión respiratoria temprana y prevenir hipoxia.

interventions.action: Evaluar nivel de conciencia usando la escala de Glasgow cada 30 min.
interventions.rationale: Cambios en la conciencia pueden indicar acumulación de opioide.

interventions.action: Mantener vía aérea permeable y posicionar al paciente en decúbito lateral si hay riesgo de aspiración.
interventions.rationale: Facilita la ventilación y reduce el riesgo de aspiración.

interventions.action: Administrar naloxona según orden médica si la frecuencia respiratoria <12 rpm o SpO₂ <92%.
interventions.rationale: Revertir rápidamente los efectos depresores del opioide.

interventions.action: Registrar todos los signos vitales y cualquier intervención en la hoja de enfermería.
interventions.rationale: Documentación precisa permite seguimiento y evaluación del plan de cuidados.

en.summary: Membrane proteins that bind opioids and modulate pain transmission and other physiological functions.
key_points: They are primarily located in the CNS and gastrointestinal tract.
Three clinical subtypes: μ (mu), κ (kappa), and δ (delta).
Activation produces analgesia, sedation, and respiratory depression.
Chronic use leads to tolerance, dependence, and possible withdrawal syndrome.
Antagonists block the receptors and reverse overdose.

mechanism: Opioids bind to the active site of the receptor and inhibit the release of excitatory neurotransmitters.
Activation of μ reduces nociceptive transmission in the spinal cord.
κ and δ modulate pain perception and emotional response.
Signaling decreases adenylate cyclase activity and opens K⁺ channels, hyperpolarizing the neuron.
nursing_care: Assess respiratory rate and level of consciousness before and after administering opioids.
Monitor SpO₂ and blood pressure every 15‑30 min during the acute phase.
Hold the dose and notify the physician if respiratory rate <12 breaths/min or SpO₂ <92%.
Keep resuscitation equipment and naloxone readily available.
Document signs of respiratory depression, excessive drowsiness, or nausea.
patient_teaching: Inform that analgesia may be accompanied by drowsiness and constipation.
Teach not to combine opioids with alcohol, benzodiazepines, or other CNS depressants.
Explain the importance of reporting difficulty breathing or changes in consciousness.
Advise not to share medication and to store opioids in a secure location.
antidote_overdose: Naloxone 0.4‑2 mg IV/IM/SC; repeat every 2‑3 min until respiratory depression reverses.
Provide ventilatory support if breathing does not quickly resume.

care_plans.diagnosis: Risk for decreased cardiac tissue perfusion
outcomes: Respiratory pattern: respiratory rate ≥12 breaths/min in 24 h

interventions.action: Monitor respiratory rate every 2 min during the first hour after dosing.
interventions.rationale: Detect early respiratory depression and prevent hypoxia.

interventions.action: Assess level of consciousness using the Glasgow Coma Scale every 30 min.
interventions.rationale: Changes in consciousness may indicate opioid accumulation.

interventions.action: Maintain a clear airway and position the patient in lateral decubitus if aspiration risk exists.
interventions.rationale: Facilitates ventilation and reduces aspiration risk.

interventions.action: Administer naloxone per physician order if respiratory rate <12 breaths/min or SpO₂ <92%.
Record all vital signs and interventions on the nursing chart.
interventions.rationale: Accurate documentation allows monitoring and evaluation of the care plan.

summary.0.quote: When activated, these receptors located throughout the CNS help modulate painful signals from peripheral tissues to alter pain perception and heighten the pain threshold.

key_points.1.quote: Opioids produce many of their desired therapeutic effects and potentially life-threatening adverse effects via the opioid receptors, including the mu, delta, and kappa receptors.

key_points.3.quote: Tolerance and physical dependence will occur in nearly all clients receiving chronic opioid therapy, but only some will go on to develop an opioid use disorder.

key_points.4.quote: Naloxone is the prototypical mu opioid receptor antagonist used to rapidly reverse the life-threatening effects of opioid overdose.

sections.mechanism.2.quote: When activated, these receptors located throughout the CNS help modulate painful signals from peripheral tissues to alter pain perception and heighten the pain threshold.

sections.nursing_care.0.quote: Assess for changes in level of consciousness and respirations.

sections.nursing_care.3.quote: Ensure that naloxone is readily available in the event of opioid toxicity or overdose.

sections.patient_teaching.1.quote: nurses should instruct clients not to mix opioids with other CNS depressants, including sedatives, alcohol, and muscle relaxants, because this interaction will increase the risk for potentially fatal respiratory failure.

sections.patient_teaching.2.quote: Assess for changes in level of consciousness and respirations.

sections.antidote_overdose.0.quote: Intranasal spray: 4–8 mg in one nostril every 2–3 minutes until medical assistance is available.

sections.antidote_overdose.1.quote: Watch for adverse effects, including sedation, ataxia, slurred speech, and shallow breathing, which could require the use of antidotal therapy or respiratory support.
